abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

sections.body: The paper argues that offline replay of recorded interactions cannot show how assistant responses change later user behavior and task outcomes. It proposes three parts: executable cooking, household, and mobile-interface environments with human-aligned action spaces; a persona-conditioned user harness built on a VLM that inserts out-of-plan events; and execution traces scored for task completion, error detection, and interaction quality. The authors instantiate this as IVG-Bench. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes 53.4% of tasks in time. A proof-of-concept GRPO run on Qwen3.5-4B improves in-time success by 8.9 percentage points after 12 updates on held-out development-validation scenarios.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Interactive Visual Gym evaluates visual assistants in closed loop, where simulated users respond to guidance, rather than by offline replay.

sections.body: The related work covers three areas. Streaming visual assistance benchmarks typically score a model against a prerecorded trajectory. Embodied and multimodal gyms place agents in simulated worlds, but the evaluated model selects its own actions. Digital interaction benchmarks pair tool-using agents with simulated users and verify outcomes from application state; tau-Voice extends this to voice, and BASIS trains and evaluates visual interaction models in Alexa Arena. The authors note that simulated users can diverge systematically from people and require validation. Their framework instead evaluates response-contingent rollouts for physical tasks.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related benchmarks mostly score visual assistants on prerecorded trajectories, or let the evaluated model choose its own actions in simulated worlds.

sections.body: The simulators are CookSim, built from scratch; VHSim, adapted from VirtualHome; and ScreenSim, which replicates the iPhone 17 Settings interface. Each exposes a semantic action space, such as 'go to the nearest pan', that an LLM grounding module maps to simulator objects. World state is a scene graph, and task progress is tracked through sub-goal conditions. The simulated user is a VLM agent with instructions for four persona axes. The harness schedules out-of-plan events and takes control of the action queue to enact them. Measured assistant latency is converted into simulation ticks. Metrics are in-time success against a completion budget, error detection recall, and five rubric-based interaction-quality dimensions scored by two LLM judges against world state.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Three simulators use semantic actions and scene-graph progress tracking, with a VLM user harness that injects scheduled errors and personas.

sections.body: IVG-Bench contains 315 scenarios: 150 in CookSim, 75 in VHSim, and 90 in ScreenSim. Each specifies a task, a user persona, and scheduled events triggered by task progress. Four classes of assistant are evaluated, including frontier API models, real-time streaming API models, and open-weight streaming and non-streaming VLMs. Gemini 4 Argon is the best-performing model, completing 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments. A human study reports 78.5% agreement between the interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. Simulated users reproduce human behavioral differences across most persona axes. They do, however, speak to assistants much more often than human participants.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across 315 scenarios, the best assistant completes 53.4% of tasks in time, and its interaction-quality metric shows 78.5% agreement with participant preferences.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the framework as closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. It states that current vision-language models show substantial limitations as reliable assistants across the three domains. The interaction approach is said to be validated by a human study, and a preliminary reinforcement-learning experiment is said to show that the environments can improve assistant performance. The ethics statement adds that simulator performance should not be taken as evidence that an assistant is safe for real-world use. The reproducibility statement points to appendices for construction, settings, prompts, and training configuration.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Current vision-language models fall short as reliable assistants, and a preliminary reinforcement-learning run shows the environments can improve one.

sections.body: Appendix A fixes the assistant to Gemini 3.7 Flash and varies the simulated-user model on 90 CookSim episodes. In-time success is 28.9% with Gemini 3.1 Pro, 23.3% with GPT-6 Astra, 21.1% with Gemini 3.7 Flash, and 2.2% with Qwen3.8-27B. GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 3.7 Flash give similar results, while Gemini 3.1 Pro differs somewhat. Appendix B repeats each assistant three times under fixed two-tick and measured delay, reporting population standard deviations. For Gemini 4 Argon under fixed two-tick delay, in-time success is 60.9 ± 2.3 in CookSim. The authors note that local open-weight models may struggle to follow the complex instructions needed to elicit the intended user behavior.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix reports sensitivity to the simulated-user model and run-to-run variation over three runs for CookSim and VHSim.
